E064-01.notes: Colon introduces the explanatory phrase 'on horseback'. A: semicolon before a non-clause. B: colon splits preposition from object. D: needless commas. A dash would also work, but no option offers one.

E064-02.notes: After substitution: 'most of whom were women' (object of 'of'). C gives 'most of who', which is ungrammatical and the main trap. A and D create comma splices or run-on structures inside the subject.

E064-03.notes: A leaves a fragment ('Where no car could go.'). B: semicolon before a dependent clause. C: the colon is unjustified. D works as a restrictive relative clause.

E064-04.notes: Dangling modifier: only B makes 'the librarians' the subject. In A, C and D the subject is the trails, danger or the trails.

E064-05.notes: The narrative is in the simple past. A and B are present perfect and do not fit the 1930s past context; B also disagrees with 'riders'. D leaves the clause with no finite verb.

E064-06.notes: Contrast: the materials arrived damaged, yet the librarians kept them. 'Therefore' is illogical, and 'For example' and 'Likewise' do not fit.

E064-07.notes: Digression about the history of quilting. C's reasoning is false because there is no contradiction. A and B misstate the sentence.

E064-08.notes: Redundancy. D is the only choice that is not redundant; it is also the shortest, so 'pick the shortest' gets it right, which is normal for ACT redundancy items.

E064-09.notes: Idiom: 'asked their children to read aloud to them'. B, C and D are unidiomatic.

E064-10.notes: The essay names the WPA, 1935 and eastern Kentucky, so D is false. A misdescribes the essay's focus (nationwide jobs), and B describes only one paragraph. Facts check out: 1935-1943, riders mostly women, donated and mended materials, scrapbooks.

E064-11.notes: B creates 'below ... below the level' (redundant and confusing). C has awkward word order ('tucked also roads'). D uses commas to split the verb from its object. Facts: 1858 Greensward Plan by Olmsted and Vaux and sunken transverse roads are accurate.

flags.note: Factual nuance in sentence 7: Seneca Village was majority African American, with a notably high rate of property ownership, but many residents were renters and there were also Irish and German residents. 'A community of mostly African American homeowners' slightly overstates this. Safer wording: 'a community of mostly African American residents, many of them property owners'.

E064-12.notes: A plain plural is needed: 'homeowners'. A and B wrongly make it possessive, and C is singular. The same passage also has a comma splice in sentence 1 and a wrong comma before 'were' in sentence 8, which are presumably tested in other items.
